items.prompt: What kind of animal is a firefly?

options.label: A beetle
options.feedback: It has hard wing cases like any other beetle.

options.label: A fly
options.feedback: The name misleads. It is not a fly at all.

options.label: A moth
options.feedback: Moths have scaled wings and no wing cases.

options.label: A small wasp
options.feedback: Wasps have a narrow waist and no wing cases.

items.ok_line: A beetle, despite two misleading names.
items.ko_line: Look at the hard covers folded over its wings. Which group does that?
items.exp_title: Neither a fly nor a worm
items.exp_text: Fireflies are beetles of the family Lampyridae, with the hardened front wings that define the group. The other common name, glow-worm, is equally misleading: it usually refers to the wingless female or to the larva, both of which glow and neither of which is a worm. Around two thousand species are known, and not all of them light up as adults.

items.prompt: Where on a firefly's body is the light produced?

options.label: In the last segments of the abdomen
options.feedback: A pale patch of tissue at the rear.

options.label: In the eyes
options.feedback: Its eyes are large but produce no light.

options.label: In the wing cases
options.feedback: Those are hard and opaque.

options.label: In the antennae
options.feedback: The antennae sense; they do not shine.

items.ok_line: The tail end, and you can see the pale patch by day.
items.ko_line: Watch a firefly flash and note which end of the body lights up.
items.exp_text: The light organ occupies the last two or three abdominal segments, visible in daylight as a pale creamy patch. Behind the light-producing cells lies a reflective layer packed with crystals that throws the glow outward instead of letting it waste inside the body. The outer cuticle over the organ carries a microscopic pattern of scales that lets more light escape — an arrangement engineers copied to improve LED efficiency.

items.prompt: How does a firefly switch its light on and off so sharply?

options.label: By controlling the oxygen supply
options.feedback: No oxygen, no reaction, no light.

options.label: By covering the organ with a flap
options.feedback: There is no shutter of any kind.

options.label: By changing its body temperature
options.feedback: Temperature is not what gates the reaction.

options.label: By squeezing out a fresh chemical
options.feedback: The fuel is already in place and waiting.

items.ok_line: Oxygen is the switch, and it can be cut in a fraction of a second.
items.ko_line: The reaction needs three things. Which of them could be turned on and off quickly?
items.exp_text: The fuel and the enzyme sit ready in the light organ; what is rationed is oxygen, delivered through fine air tubes. Nitric oxide released by the insect's nerves briefly stops the surrounding cells from consuming oxygen, so a pulse floods through to the light cells and the lantern fires. Cut it off and the light stops within milliseconds — precise enough to send a coded pattern.

items.prompt: What does a female firefly's answering flash tell the male?

options.label: That she is the right species
options.feedback: The delay before her reply identifies her.

options.label: How far away she is
options.feedback: He judges distance by brightness, not by timing.

options.label: How old she is
options.feedback: Age is not carried in the signal.

options.label: That danger is nearby
options.feedback: The exchange is courtship, not alarm.

items.ok_line: The delay is the password, and it is measured in fractions of a second.
items.ko_line: She waits a precise interval before answering. Why would the interval matter?
items.exp_text: The male flies and flashes his species' pattern; a perched female answers after a delay that is specific to her species — often around two seconds, and accurate to a fraction of one. He reads the delay, not the brightness, and only approaches if it matches. Where several species share a meadow, the timing is what keeps them from courting the wrong partner.

items.prompt: How does a Photuris female trap males of other species?

options.label: She copies their answering flash
options.feedback: The male approaches, and she eats him.

options.label: She builds a web to catch them
options.feedback: Beetles do not spin webs.

options.label: She releases their species' scent
options.feedback: The trap is visual, not chemical.

options.label: She waits at their nest sites
options.feedback: Fireflies have no nests.

items.ok_line: She learns another species' reply and answers with it.
items.ko_line: The whole courtship runs on flash codes. What would a predator do with that?
items.exp_text: Females of the genus Photuris mimic the reply timing of other firefly species, luring the males in and eating them. They can switch between several codes depending on who is flashing nearby. There is a second motive: their prey carry defensive chemicals called lucibufagins that Photuris cannot make itself, and eating a male supplies them — which she then passes to her own eggs.

items.prompt: What is a glow-worm, in most cases?

options.label: A wingless female firefly
options.feedback: She glows steadily from the ground to attract a flying male.

options.label: A worm that has eaten fireflies
options.feedback: Eating a glowing animal does not make you glow.

options.label: A separate species of earthworm
options.feedback: No earthworm produces light.

options.label: A caterpillar that shines
options.feedback: The glowing larva is a beetle grub, not a caterpillar.

items.ok_line: The same beetle, in the form that never flies.
items.ko_line: It is not a worm, and it is closely related to something already discussed here.
items.exp_text: In many European species the female never develops wings. She climbs a grass stem at dusk and shines a steady green light upward, and males patrol overhead looking for her — the reverse of the flashing courtship of American fireflies. The larvae glow too, and hunt slugs and snails, paralysing prey many times their own size before eating it over several days.

items.prompt: What is remarkable about the fireflies of some Southeast Asian rivers?

options.label: Whole trees flash in unison
options.feedback: Thousands of insects on and off together.

options.label: They flash in every colour
options.feedback: The colour range is narrow, mostly yellow-green.

options.label: They glow continuously all night
options.feedback: The point is that they pulse rather than glow.

options.label: They fly only during the day
options.feedback: A daytime flash would be invisible.

items.ok_line: Thousands of beetles, one rhythm, whole trees pulsing together.
items.ko_line: The remarkable part is not the light itself but the coordination.
items.exp_title: Thousands of insects on one beat
items.exp_text: Along mangrove rivers in Malaysia and Thailand, males gather in particular trees and flash in unison, sometimes tens of thousands together, and whole riverbanks pulse two or three times a second for hours. Each insect adjusts its own rhythm slightly towards its neighbours, and synchrony emerges without any leader. It is the same mathematics that makes pendulum clocks on a shared wall fall into step.

items.prompt: What do New Zealand cave glow-worms use their light for?

options.label: To lure insects into hanging threads
options.feedback: The prey flies at the light and sticks.

options.label: To attract a mate in the dark
options.feedback: It is the larva that glows, and it does not mate.

options.label: To see the cave walls
options.feedback: The light is far too weak to see by.

options.label: To warn bats away
options.feedback: Bats are not the concern in those caves.

items.ok_line: A ceiling of false stars, over threads of glue.
items.ko_line: It hangs sticky threads below itself. What is the light for, then?
items.exp_title: A false sky over a trap
items.exp_text: The larva of a fungus gnat hangs from a cave ceiling and lowers dozens of silk threads beaded with mucus, then glows. Insects hatched in the cave fly towards what looks like open sky, hit the threads and are hauled up. A hungry larva shines brighter than a well-fed one. Caves at Waitomo hold enough of them to read by, and the effect is close to a starry night indoors.

items.prompt: Why do firefly eggs and larvae glow as well?

options.label: It warns predators they taste foul
options.feedback: They carry defensive chemicals, and advertise it.

options.label: It helps the parents find them
options.feedback: Adults do not tend their eggs.

options.label: It keeps the eggs warm
options.feedback: The light gives off almost no heat.

options.label: It attracts food to the larvae
options.feedback: The larvae hunt snails, which ignore light.

items.ok_line: A label, not a lure: do not eat me.
items.ko_line: The egg cannot mate, cannot hunt and cannot flee. What is left for a signal to do?
items.exp_title: The glow began as a warning
items.exp_text: Fireflies at every stage — eggs, larvae, pupae and adults — carry bitter defensive chemicals, and the glow appears to have started as a warning label rather than a courtship signal. Larvae glow in all species, including those whose adults do not, which suggests the warning came first and the mating code was built on top of it much later.

items.prompt: Why are fireflies becoming harder to find in many places?

options.label: Artificial light drowns their signals
options.feedback: They cannot see each other's flashes against it.

options.label: They are being eaten by birds
options.feedback: Birds mostly avoid them; they taste foul.

options.label: The nights have become too cold
options.feedback: Cold slows them but is not the main cause.

options.label: They have run out of food
options.feedback: Snails and slugs remain plentiful.

items.ok_line: Their whole language is written in flashes, and the page is no longer dark.
items.ko_line: Their courtship depends entirely on being able to see a small light. What ruins that?
items.exp_text: Firefly courtship depends on faint flashes being visible against darkness. Where streetlights and floodlights raise the background, males and females can no longer read each other and fail to pair. Studies find fewer flashes and fewer matings near lit areas, and the loss of damp grassland where larvae hunt snails compounds it. Turning lights off during the season measurably helps.
